steps.notes: Minimum-image distance; correct impl passes all 3 tests.

Truncated-shifted LJ; correct impl passes. Test 0 (r=rc=1, sigma=1) is degenerate (target 0.0) but harmless: r<rc and r<=rc conventions both give 0 there. Docstring mentions a nonexistent optional Yukawa potential (copy-paste noise).
Correct all-pairs E_pot FAILS test 2. Target bit-matches sum over CONSECUTIVE array rows (i,i+1) only ('chain' energy). Chain impl passes officially.

Standard convention (r = r_i - r_j, F_i = -dV/dr*rhat) FAILS with exactly negated values; opposite convention (+dV/dr*rhat, i.e. r points i->j) PASSES. Direction of input displacement never specified; docstring even types r as a float distance while tests pass a 3-vector.

Correct pairwise vector forces FAIL (shape crash on test 1, wrong direction everywhere). Targets bit-match chain-only (i,i+1) forces with the signed SCALAR +dV/dr broadcast across x,y,z. Test 1 also passes N=2 with a 3-row positions array (target shape (2,3)).
Velocity Verlet targets inherit the broken chain scalar-broadcast forces (velocity deltas isotropic [c,c,c]). Correct implementation FAILS all tests; bug-reproducing implementation PASSES.

Correct vectorized Anderson-NVT (using len(arrays)=216) PASSES, margins ~10x inside the 5% bands. But trivial no-simulation constants ALSO pass, chain-broken dynamics also pass, and a correct impl that trusts N=200 for T normalization FAILS (arrays carry 216 particles).

findings.evidence: Docstring: 'Calculate the total potential energy of a system using the truncated and shifted Lennard-Jones potential'; prompt: 'get the total energy of the whole system ... sum of local energies'. The h5 target for test 2 (10 particles, rc=5) is -0.0010667416018009025, but the correct all-pairs sum (min-image, truncated-shifted) is -0.30289870210724418 -- steptest FAIL on a correct implementation. The target is reproduced BIT-EXACTLY by summing E_ij only over consecutive array rows: sum_i E_ij(dist(xyz[i],xyz[i+1],L)) = -0.0010667416018009025 (review/work/80/impl_b3.py passes officially). Tests 0 and 1 cannot discriminate (test 0 has N=2; test 1's pairs are all at r>=rc, target 0.0). The reference treated the background phrase 'the energy between the two atoms next to each other' as adjacent ARRAY INDICES -- physically meaningless for a 3D periodic fluid and contradicting the step's own 'total potential energy of a system'.
findings.suggested_fix: Regenerate the test-2 target with the standard all-pairs sum over i<j of the truncated-shifted LJ at min-image distances (-0.30289870210724418 for the given configuration), and reword the background sentence to 'energy between pairs of atoms within the cutoff'.

findings.evidence: Prompt: 'calculates the forces between two particles whose three dimensional displacement is r' -- the direction of the displacement (r_i - r_j vs r_j - r_i) is never stated; docstring even contradicts the prompt by typing 'r (float): The distance between particles i and j' while all tests pass a 3-vector, and the return doc says 'The force vector experienced by particle i due to particle j'. The step's own background gives F = -dV/d(r-vec). Targets encode f = +dV/dr * r/|r| (e.g. test 1: target [0.00220958, -0.0029461, 0.00368263] = +dVdr * rhat), i.e. r must be read as pointing FROM i TO j. The equally standard reading r = r_i - r_j yields exactly the negated vector and FAILS steptest (verified: impl_a FAIL, impl_b PASS). A competent solver faces a 50/50 sign guess. Docstring also mentions a nonexistent 'Yukawa potential' option.
findings.suggested_fix: State in the docstring: 'r: 3D displacement vector from particle i to particle j (r_j - r_i)'; fix the float->vector type description and delete the Yukawa sentence.

findings.evidence: Prompt/docstring demand 'net force VECTORS acting on each particle ... in zJ/nm' from 'pairwise interactions with its neighbors'. Every row of every nonzero target has identical x=y=z components (test 1 row0 = [6.6107e-4]*3; test 2 rows all isotropic), which no genuine pair-force sum can produce (forces must lie along inter-particle displacements). Targets are reproduced exactly by: looping only over CONSECUTIVE pairs (i,i+1) and adding the signed SCALAR +dV/dr (at the min-image distance) broadcast across all three components -- verified: chain-scalar impl_b PASSES steptest; correct vector forces FAIL; all-pairs scalar broadcast also FAILS (test 2 mismatch ~3.7e3). The reference evidently passed the scalar dist() output into f_ij, whose r/|r| silently became 1, and only chained neighbors. No physically correct implementation can pass tests 1-2.
findings.suggested_fix: Regenerate targets with a correct all-pairs loop using min-image displacement VECTORS: f_xyz[i] += f_ij(vec_ij), f_xyz[j] -= f_ij(vec_ij).

findings.evidence: Docstring contract: 'xyz : A NumPy array with shape (N, 3)'. Test 1 passes N=2 while positions has THREE rows; the frozen target has shape (2,3). An implementation that (reasonably) iterates over len(xyz) returns shape (3,3) and crashes the assert: 'ValueError: operands could not be broadcast together with shapes (3,3) (2,3)' (observed running impl_a). Only implementations that allocate (N,3) and silently ignore the extra row can pass. Even with the D7 chain bug fixed, this test would still fail contract-faithful solutions.
findings.suggested_fix: Make test 1 self-consistent: either set N=3 or drop the third position row, and regenerate the target.

findings.evidence: Targets were generated with the broken step-5 forces: in test 0 the velocity increments are isotropic (new_v - v = [1.2202e-4, 1.2202e-4, 1.2202e-4] and its negation), impossible for real LJ forces along the displacement [-0.045, -2.925, 0.388]. A textbook velocity-Verlet step using correct pairwise vector forces FAILS steptest on all tests; the same Verlet code using the reverse-engineered chain scalar-broadcast forces PASSES (impl_a FAIL / impl_b PASS). The defect is inherited from 80.5's reference bug (D9 propagation), so a solver who implements the documented physics correctly is scored wrong on two consecutive steps.
findings.suggested_fix: Regenerate 80.6 targets from a reference whose forces() computes genuine all-pairs vector forces.

findings.evidence: Docstring: 'N: The number of particles in the system. init_positions: 2D array ... with shape (N,3)'. The tests call initialize_fcc(200) which builds ceil(200^(1/3))^3 = 216 particles, then pass N=200 with (216,3) arrays. A physically correct implementation that trusts the contract and normalizes instantaneous temperature by N (T_inst = m*sum(v^2)/(3*N*kB)) overestimates T by 216/200 = 1.08 > the 1.05 band and FAILS (verified: impl_a7_N FAIL, while the identical code normalizing by len(arrays) PASSES). Other contract-trusting patterns crash outright (np.zeros((N,3)) + full-array loops -> IndexError; (216,3)+(200,3) broadcasts -> ValueError). Pass/fail hinges on an undocumented choice of which particle count to believe.
findings.suggested_fix: Use N values whose cube root is an integer (e.g. N=216) in all three tests, or have initialize_fcc truncate to exactly N positions.

findings.evidence: The only assertions are two 5%-band statistics: mean(instant_T_array[400:]) vs T and 1/mean(intercollision_times) vs nu; all three frozen targets are (True, True). A no-simulation stub returning instant_T_array=np.full(num_steps,T), intercollision_times=np.full(1000,1/nu), zeros for energy and the unchanged inputs PASSES all tests officially (impl_t7 PASS). An MD with the completely wrong chain scalar-broadcast forces also PASSES (impl_b7), since the Anderson thermostat bookkeeping alone fixes both statistics. E_total_array, positions and velocities are returned but never checked. The tests verify thermostat bookkeeping only, not molecular dynamics.
findings.suggested_fix: Additionally assert a deterministic physical quantity, e.g. seed the RNG in the test and check E_total_array/positions against frozen arrays, or at least check energy conservation between collisions.

findings.evidence: The MD_NVT docstring describes a different function: 'Integrate the equations of motion using the velocity Verlet algorithm, with the inclusion of the Berendsen thermostat and barostat for temperature and pressure control' and 'Returns: tuple -- Updated positions and velocities of all particles, and the possibly modified box length after barostat adjustment.' The prompt/background specify an ANDERSON thermostat (NVT, no barostat) and the return line carries five values: return(E_total_array, instant_T_array, positions, velocities, intercollision_times) -- none of the three arrays is documented anywhere. A solver following the docstring would implement Berendsen rescaling (no collisions -> intercollision_times undefined -> fail), and the semantics of intercollision_times (pooled per-particle waiting times between successive collisions of the SAME particle) is only inferable from the background's P(t;nu)=nu*exp(-nu*t); the also-plausible 'time between successive collision events anywhere in the system' reading is off by a factor ~N and fails the nu band.
findings.suggested_fix: Rewrite the docstring for the Anderson NVT function: remove Berendsen/barostat text and document each of the five returns (per-step total energy array, per-step instantaneous temperature array, final positions, final velocities, pooled per-particle intercollision waiting times).

findings.evidence: The Anderson thermostat is inherently stochastic and the tests neither seed numpy's RNG nor allow for it; the official verdict depends on unseeded np.random draws. Measured margins for a correct implementation over 3 seeds x 3 configs: relative T error <= 0.0050 vs band 0.05, relative nu error <= 0.0059 vs band 0.05 (~10x headroom, 216 particles x 2000 steps x ~0.2 collision prob), so realistic flake probability is small, but the score is not strictly reproducible.
findings.suggested_fix: Seed the RNG at the top of each test case (np.random.seed(k)) -- harmless given band-style asserts, and makes scoring reproducible.

findings.evidence: A correct solver who reuses the loop-based step-5 forces() (the structure the problem teaches) needs 2 force evaluations x 2000 steps x 3 tests = 12000 calls on 216 particles; one call measures 0.13 s here, extrapolating to ~26 min for the joint script, at/over the official 1800 s limit. The reference never faced this because its chain forces are O(N). Only solvers who independently vectorize the O(N^2) force loop run in ~30 s.
findings.suggested_fix: Reduce num_steps or N in the 80.7 tests, or raise the per-step time limit, so a straightforward loop-based correct solution can finish.

findings.evidence: E_ij docstring: 'Calculate the combined truncated and shifted Lennard-Jones potential energy and, if specified, the truncated and shifted Yukawa potential energy' and 'Returns: float: The combined potential energy ... considering the specified potentials' -- but no Yukawa parameters exist anywhere in the problem (copy-paste from another problem). Same stray Yukawa text appears in 80.4's f_ij docstring. Confusing but the LJ-only reading passes.
findings.suggested_fix: Delete the Yukawa sentences from the 80.2 and 80.4 docstrings.

overall_assessment: Problem 80 is one of the most defective problems reviewed: the reference solution that generated the frozen targets computes interactions only between CONSECUTIVE array indices ('chain') and, for forces, broadcasts a signed scalar +dV/dr across x,y,z instead of projecting along the displacement. As a result, steps 80.3, 80.5 and 80.6 are blockers -- a physically correct implementation provably fails all of them (and the bug was reproduced bit-exactly), while 80.4 requires winning an unstated 50/50 sign-convention guess. Step 80.7 then inverts the failure mode: its purely statistical (and unseeded) band checks pass a no-simulation stub and the chain-broken dynamics alike, while failing a correct implementation that trusts the documented N (tests pass N=200 with 216-particle arrays). Only 80.1 and 80.2 score fairly; the problem needs its targets regenerated from a corrected reference before it can measure anything meaningful.
